similar_scenes.name: Blues funky y blues clásico
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: Del grito de los esclavos a las fiestas de sábado por la noche en los campos de algodón, el blues rural cumplía la misma función que la música africana. Con la urbanización de la Primera Guerra Mundial llegó el primer blues grabado, el «blues clásico» de Bessie y Mamie Smith, a menudo picante («Need a Little Sugar in My Bowl»), y el hot jazz de Louis Armstrong, que asustó a los críticos y abrió el mercado de los «race records».
similar_scenes.family: Raíces: blues, jazz, gospel y R&B

similar_scenes.name: Rhythm and blues
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: En los cuarenta, los combos de jump como el Tympany Five de Louis Jordan sustituyeron a las big bands: baile, ritmo, scat, solo de saxo. Gente que trabajaba duro todo el día necesitaba música fuerte y con alma: un grito sincero, un saxo, una guitarra rockera. Su «misma vulgaridad», dice LeRoi Jones, aseguraba su conexión con la vida de la gente, y esa vulgaridad fue el ingrediente principal del funk. Despreciado por los intelectuales como mal jazz, el R&B dio a Chuck Berry, Little Richard y Bo Diddley, inspiró el rock and roll y la invasión británica, y en el chitlin circuit fue el útero del funk. Con Live at the Apollo de James Brown (1962, disco de oro) el R&B se hizo mayor; de él salieron Ray Charles, Brown y Aretha Franklin.
similar_scenes.family: Raíces: blues, jazz, gospel y R&B

similar_scenes.name: Santana
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: Nacida en las jam sessions de garaje del Mission latino de San Francisco, la banda multirracial y cargada de percusión de Carlos Santana (Gregg Rolie al órgano, Michael Shrieve a la batería, José Areas y Mike Carabello a las congas) arrasó en Woodstock gracias a Bill Graham y vendió un millón con su primer disco para Columbia. Ritmos latinos, folk mexicano y jazz afrocubano, y una guitarra que sostiene notas hacia nuevos horizontes; después, jazz con Chick Corea y John McLaughlin.
similar_scenes.family: Funk psicodélico y black rock: Sly, Hendrix

similar_scenes.name: Blues rock británico
similar_scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
similar_scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
similar_scenes.desc: La «gramática» del heavy: su estructura de canción, sus progresiones y sus riffs vienen del blues eléctrico urbano de Muddy Waters y Howlin’ Wolf, pero de segunda mano, ya «rockeado» por los grupos británicos de guitarra. El gran mediador son los Yardbirds y su sucesión de solistas (Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck y Jimmy Page), que veneraban a los bluesmen negros sin imitarlos servilmente. Cream (y Clapton, según él mismo) inventa el solo largo para estirar media hora de repertorio, y el público lo convierte en convención. El virtuosismo de la guitarra solista es la mayor herencia del blues rock al heavy.
similar_scenes.family: Raíces: blues rock, psicodelia y hard rock

similar_scenes.name: Country blues
similar_scenes.author: Ted Gioia
similar_scenes.desc: La cara liberadora y dionisíaca del ritmo africano: un medio para expresar dolor, opresión y deseo sin autocompasión, con un efecto catártico comparable al de la tragedia. Lo conocemos por grabaciones a partir de los años veinte. Forma de doce compases (tónica, dominante, subdominante) con blue notes que oscilan entre tercera mayor y menor, y estrofa AAB; pero los cantantes del campo alargan o acortan los compases a su antojo porque cantan solos con su guitarra. Charlie Patton, más antiguo y ligado a la plantación, dialoga con su guitarra; Blind Lemon Jefferson canta agudo y fino en Texas; Leadbelly, descubierto en una cárcel por los Lomax, acaba en Nueva York; Robert Johnson, tardío y casi desconocido en vida, se convierte en el paradigma del Delta. Gioia duda del origen en los griots africanos: el blues es un tipo de canción nuevo, nacido en el Sur.
similar_scenes.family: Raíces: África, blues, ragtime y espirituales

similar_scenes.name: Blues clásico
similar_scenes.author: Ted Gioia
similar_scenes.desc: Una forma más aculturada del blues: doce compases estrictos, banda en lugar de guitarra, elementos del jazz, los minstrels, el circo y el vodevil, y un punto de vista femenino sobre el amor no correspondido, lascivo o maltratador. El blues pasa de la calle al teatro y la carpa, empujado por el negocio discográfico: el disco de Mamie Smith de 1920 vende un millón y las compañías lanzan los race records y mandan cazatalentos al Sur. Ma Rainey, de los espectáculos itinerantes de minstrels, graba más de cien discos con Armstrong o Coleman Hawkins; su protegida Bessie Smith, la mayor cantante del género, triunfa con «Down Hearted Blues» (1923), llena teatros sin amplificación y canta de sexo con doble sentido. W. C. Handy lleva el blues a las partituras de Tin Pan Alley. Al lado de Armstrong ya se oye cómo el jazz tiende a ornamentar mientras el blues se queda en la emoción desnuda.
similar_scenes.family: Raíces: África, blues, ragtime y espirituales

similar_scenes.name: Blues revival y blues-rock
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: John Mayall define con Bluesbreakers (con Eric Clapton) el rhythm'n'blues tocado por blancos europeos, el blues-rock, y siembra el progresivo con sus discos de jazz y lounge. Su equivalente americano es Al Kooper (Blues Project, Supersession, Blood Sweat & Tears). Cream, el primer power-trio, cambia la cara del rock británico con improvisación de jazz, distorsión y solos interminables; Fleetwood Mac de Peter Green y Ten Years After llevan del blues al hard rock. En San Francisco, Janis Joplin, Steve Miller y Santana; en Los Ángeles, Taj Mahal y Ry Cooder reconstruyen las tradiciones; Bob Seger casa el grito soul con el Detroit obrero.

podcast.title: Development and Spread of Blues (c. 1870-1950s)
podcast.body: Concurrently with jazz, the blues developed in the US South, with roots as early as 1870, becoming widely heard by 1901-1902, facilitated by gramophones and phonographs. Simpler in arrangement than jazz, often requiring little more than a guitar and a voice, blues found its base in "Jukejoints," African American gathering places for music, dance, and drink. These venues formed the "Chitlin Circuit," a touring network for musicians stretching from Florida to New York City's Apollo Theater and Cotton Club. The blues fused with country, western, and hillbilly music, leading to the birth of rock'n'roll by the early 1950s. "And by the early 1950s, we have a descendant called Rock'n'Roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Dirty Blues" Records (1950s)
podcast.body: By 1952, *Jet* magazine noted an unprecedented number of "dirty blues records" on sale, often making no effort to conceal their suggestive nature. These records, using "cunning inflections" and standard "dirty record vocabulary" like "rock and roll," "writer," "grind," and "grass," were criticized for directly describing sexual activity. "Never have there been as many dirty blues records on sale as today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Please Mr. Postman" Original Conception
podcast.body: The initial idea for "Please Mr. Postman" originated as a blues song about a postman, conceived by William Garrett. Georgia Dobbins later transformed it, writing most of the lyrics and making it "less bluesy." "A friend of Georgia, William Garrett, had started a blues song about a postman, and Georgia worked on his idea, writing most of the lyrics, and recasting it as something less bluesy."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: "The Fat Man" Lyrics - Blues Trope of Body Positivity and Attraction
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew's lyrics for "The Fat Man" employ a common blues trope where a large man boasts about his attractiveness to women despite his size. "follow a standard blues trope of being fat but having the ability to attract women anyway."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: 15-Bar Blues Structure
podcast.body: The original version of "The Twist," as written by the Sensational Nightingales, was structured as a 15-bar blues. This particular structure was considered "an awkward, uncommercial number," which prompted Hank Ballard and Cal Green to adapt it. "The song as the sensational Nightingale sang it was a 15 bar blues and 15 bars is an awkward, uncommercial number."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Adaptation to 12-Bar Melody
podcast.body: Hank Ballard and the Midnighters' guitarist Cal Green, along with Ballard, took the 15-bar blues structure of "The Twist" and adapted its lyrics to a pre-existing 12-bar melody. This was done to make the song more commercially viable than its original awkward 15-bar format. "So he and the Midnighters guitarist Cal Green took the song that the Nightingale sang and fit the lyrics to a pre-existing 12 bar melody."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Backbeat Origins
podcast.body: Players in blues music had been using the backbeat rhythm, often done on drums, since the 1920s, long before it became popular in the 1950s. This demonstrates the rhythm's deep roots in African American music forms. "Players in blues and jazz music had been using that rhythm often done since the 1920s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 2: "Roll Em Pete" by Big Joe Turner

podcast.title: Blue Notes and Scale Tension
podcast.body: Blues music features "blue notes," which are microtonal pitches falling between a minor and a major. These notes are an inherent part of the genre's tension, existing beyond the standard 12-note Western scale and sometimes described as a "13th thing." "it's an inherent part of the tension of blues music. We only use a 12 note scale, but blues has that 13th thing there too, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: CBGB's Original Music Policy
podcast.body: When Hilly Crystal bought the club that would become CBGB, he initially named it to reflect his music policy, which included country, bluegrass, and blues, among "other music for uplifting gourmandizers." "He named it after his music policy, the kinds of acts he would book, country, blue grass and blues and other music for uplifting gourmandizers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: CBGB's Original Policy
podcast.body: CBGB, established in 1973, was originally named "CBGB and OMFUG" to indicate its initial musical policy, which included Blues, alongside Country and Bluegrass, and "Other Music for Uplifting Gormandizers." Despite this initial vision, the club rapidly shifted its focus to become a crucial venue for avant-garde and punk artists. "He called it CBGB an Umfug, which spells out its musical policy. Country, bluegrass, blues, and other music for uplifting Gorman Dysers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 5: (60-51)

podcast.title: Chicago Blues Sound
podcast.body: Chicago's blues music possessed a unique and identifiable regional sound, serving as a prominent example of how geographical location influenced and shaped musical expression. "Chicago's brand of blues."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: City Blues vs. Country Blues Attitude
podcast.body: An informal group of musicians around Atlantic Records, including Mickey Baker, Doc Pomus, Big Joe Turner, and King Curtis, played "sophisticated city blues and R&B." They looked down upon country bluesmen, who are now more widely recognized, as "comparatively unsophisticated musicians," viewing their music as something "anyone could do." "They were playing sophisticated city blues and R&B, and rather looked down on the country bluesmen, who are now much better known, as being comparatively unsophisticated musicians."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 49: "Love is Strange" by Mickey and Sylvia

podcast.title: Component of Indie Folk
podcast.body: Blues music is identified as one of the genres that came together in Indie Folk, contributing to its rootsy and acoustic characteristics. "This is a corner of alt rock where folk, blues, gospel, and even a little country came together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 3: The New Genres

podcast.title: Early 20th-Century Mississippi Delta Slide Guitar
podcast.body: In the early 20th century, blues players in the Mississippi Delta developed unique slide guitar techniques. Lacking proper "steels" used in Hawaiian music, they famously improvised by pressing knives or the necks of beer bottles against their guitar strings. "The earliest players didn't have proper steels used by players of the Hawaiian style. They used a knife on their strings and when a knife wasn't available, the neck of a beer bottle would do an pinch."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Suggestive Lyrics (1920s)
podcast.body: In the 1920s, early blues recordings began to feature suggestive titles and lyrics, contributing to public outrage over "dirty lyrics" in music. This trend, exemplified by songs like Tampa Red and Georgia Tom's "It's Tight Like That" (1928), indicated a growing tension between traditional morality and new forms of musical expression. "When we got to the 1920s, early blues and jazz recordings appeared with very suggestive titles and lyrics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Use of "Rocking and Rolling"
podcast.body: The terms "rocking and rolling" and "rock and roll" appeared almost exclusively among blues and R&B singers in the years following Trixie Smith's 1922 recording. This linguistic evolution within the genre laid the groundwork for the future naming of rock and roll music. "And in the coming years, those words, rocking and rolling and rocking roll, appeared in other songs, almost exclusively amongst blues and R&B singers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Electric Guitar Revolution (1950s)
podcast.body: The electric guitar revolutionized many types of popular music starting in the 1950s, including the blues. "Starting in the 1950s, it revolutionized many types of popular music, country, the blues, jazz and most of all, rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 2

podcast.title: Evolution with Electric Guitar
podcast.body: As the blues genre evolved and the electric guitar became prevalent, the slide playing technique also advanced, championed by figures like Muddy Waters and Elmore James. "With the blues evolved and the electric guitar was introduced, playing slide evolved."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Financial Motivation for Mickey Baker
podcast.body: For Mickey Baker, blues initially served as a financial opportunity rather than a passion. He transitioned from complex jazz to "bending strings" in blues because it was "far, far easier" and he could make "far more money," as he was "starving to death." "I started bending strings. I was starving to death, and the blues was just a financial thing for me then."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 49: "Love is Strange" by Mickey and Sylvia

podcast.title: Floating Lyrics Tradition
podcast.body: A significant blues tradition involved "floating lyrics," where songs were not conventional compositions with fixed lyrics but rather a melodic structure over which a singer would improvise. Singers would pull lyrics from a set of pre-existing, commonly known phrases that were known to work, allowing for flexibility and extended performances, as seen in many of Big Joe Turner's songs. "When blues singers improvised, they tend to pull out lyrics from a set of pre-existing phrases that they knew worked."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 2: "Roll Em Pete" by Big Joe Turner

podcast.title: Floating Lyrics Tradition
podcast.body: Certain lyrical phrases, such as "the train arrived 16 coaches long" (from "Warwickman Blues"), became part of a tradition of "floating lyrics" that blues singers could draw upon for their songs. "those lyrics, the train arrived 16 coaches long, became part of the floating lyrics that all blue singers could call upon."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Folk Art Form Status
podcast.body: Like country music, blues was essentially a folk art form to start with. This informal origin meant that authorship claims for songs could be difficult due to the tradition of floating lyrics and the common practice of assembling songs from pre-existing elements. "rock and roll, like blues and country before it, was essentially a folk art form to start with."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 2: "Roll Em Pete" by Big Joe Turner

podcast.title: Foundation for R&B and Rock
podcast.body: The establishment of blues as a popular recorded art form in the early 20th century, notably pioneered by artists like Mamie Smith, created fundamental groundwork for the development of R&B and, by extension, rock music approximately 30 years later. "And by doing that, it created many of the foundations of blues records that were to come, not to mention R&B, and by extension rock music some 30 plus years later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundation of Modern Rock
podcast.body: The blues, particularly through artists like Buddy Guy, forms part and parcel of the foundation of modern rock music, leading directly from the Mississippi Delta to 70s and 80s arena rock. "If you trace a straight line from the Mississippi Delta to what becomes 70s and 80s or Rainer Rock, you're going to run straight through buddy guy."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 59 - Bands and Booze on the Festival Express of 1970

podcast.title: Foundation of Rock and Roll
podcast.body: The blues is one of the primary Black Music genres from which rock and roll, and subsequently alt rock, substantially descended. "It's only right, given that rock and roll is descended substantially from Black Music, the blues, rhythm and blues, jump blues, jazz, gospel, and so many other genres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundational Element
podcast.body: The blues formed one of the core musical styles, alongside country and R&B, that contributed to the new sound gravitated towards by teenagers in the 1950s with the rise of rock and roll. "played music derived from a mix of the blues, country and R&B."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundational Influence on Modern Music
podcast.body: The blues served as a fundamental building block for many subsequent genres, influencing everything from rock and R&B to funk and hip hop, due to its distinctive structure and expressive storytelling. "They are also the foundations for everything from rock and R&B to funk and hip hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Historical Racist Criticism
podcast.body: Blues music was targeted in a British newspaper review which described it as deplorable and tribal, originating from America and stemming from the "jungle," suggesting it might be "the Negro's revenge." This criticism also linked blues with other genres like ragtime, jazz, hot cha-cha, and boogie-woogie under the same racist condemnation in 1956. "It follows ragtime, blues, jazz, hot cha-cha, and the boogie-woogie, which surely originated in the jungle. We sometimes wonder whether this is the Negro's revenge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of Women Guitarists on Blues
podcast.body: Women guitarists such as Memphis Minnie and Sister Rosetta Tharpe profoundly influenced the course of the blues, introducing different playing styles and paving the way for future rock pioneers. "sister Rosetta Tharp had a profound effect on the course of the blues."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Early Rock Bands
podcast.body: Rock bands of the 1960s and early 1970s borrowed liberally from the blues, integrating its sounds and structures into their music. This influence is also evident in the diverse genres, including blues, country, rock, and roots, found within Credence Clearwater Revival's sound, which served as a model for Heartland Rock. "And of course, rock bands of the early 60s, of the 60s, I should say, in early 70s, they borrowed liberally from the blues."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 55 - Heartland Rock is about More than the Heartland

podcast.title: Influence on Guitar Solos (N/A)
podcast.body: Blues players such as Blind, Mill, and Jefferson are cited as early examples demonstrating guitar solos, contributing to the development of this technique in popular music. "We can also look at blues players like Blind, Mill, and Jefferson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Janis Joplin
podcast.body: Janis Joplin's form of rock was heavily influenced by the Blues. "It's no secret that Janice was not only a fan of the Blues, but her own form of rock was very heavily influenced by the Blues."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 59 - Bands and Booze on the Festival Express of 1970

podcast.title: Influence on Rock and Roll
podcast.body: Blues is cited as one of the foundational genres that, when combined with country music, formed the "amalgam" that became rock and roll. "it's just like that amalgam of blues and country and whatever that became rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on U2
podcast.body: Blues music was a significant influence on U2 as they began to study and root themselves in classic American music during their time in the United States. "tenemos muchas influencias del blues."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Inspiration for Guitarists
podcast.body: The blues genre, particularly through artists like Junior Kimbrough, played a crucial role in shaping the career path of Dan Auerbach, helping him decide to dedicate himself to playing guitar. "In fact, listening to Kimbrough, while smoking a lot of dope, helped him decide to pursue the guitar full time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Malismal Use in Blues
podcast.body: While not as strictly adhered to as in more "upmarket" styles, malisma was largely avoided in blues music, with songs typically sung as written, which usually meant without multiple notes per syllable. "And this was largely the case in the blues as well as in the more upmarket styles. The rules weren't stuck too quite as firmly there, but still you'd mostly sing the song as it was written and it would largely be written without Malisma."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Origin and Characteristics
podcast.body: The blues is an African-American invention that originated in the South, characterized by simple songs recounting stories of hard lives, bad luck, real life experiences, and complex relationships between men and women. This music is also known as folk blues or rural blues. "Adjacent to that was the blues, another African-American invention that came from the South."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins of Blues and Blue Notes (c. 1870s)
podcast.body: The blues genre emerged from the US Deep South around the 1870s, following the end of slavery, drawing from slave work songs, spiritual music, and African musical traditions. It is characterized by "blue notes," which are pitches that fall between the accepted tones found on a conventional piano keyboard, also known as "bent notes." These notes represent the kind of "natural imperfections" that Pythagoras sought to eliminate from music, favoring discrete tones, while blues players embraced them. "The blues came out of the deep south beginning in about the 1870s following the end of slavery."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Civil War Spread and Delta Roots
podcast.body: Folk blues or rural blues began to spread across the Deep South following the American Civil War. The three-line stanza structure of these songs can be traced back to the field songs prevalent in the Mississippi Delta, forming foundational elements for genres like rock, R&B, funk, and hip hop. "The structure of these songs with their three line stances can trace back to the field songs in the Mississippi Delta."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prominence at Fame Recording Studios
podcast.body: Fame Recording Studios in Sheffield, Alabama, developed a strong reputation as the ideal location for blues musicians to make records. "A Gainer reputation is the place for soul, blues, and R&B musicians to make records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radio Broadcasts (1920s)
podcast.body: Radio broadcasting in the 1920s enabled the live performance of blues music to reach widespread audiences directly in their homes. This expansion of reach through radio contributed significantly to the genre's growing popularity and accessibility. "People across vast distances could enjoy classical music, opera, hymns, jazz, and blues simply by turning on their radios."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

podcast.title: Rediscovery by British Bands
podcast.body: In the early 1960s, American blues records were rediscovered by young British bands like The Rolling Stones and Cream, who paid close attention to artists such as Buddy Guy. "In the early 1960s, American blues records were kind of rediscovered by the British bands like the Rolling Stones and Cream."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 59 - Bands and Booze on the Festival Express of 1970

podcast.title: Renewed Interest (Late 1980s/Early 1990s)
podcast.body: After a period where blues artists like Buddy Guy commercially stalled, there was a renewed public interest in blues music in the late 1980s and early 1990s. "But things turned around a bit with that renewed interest in blues that we saw in the late 80s and early 90s."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 59 - Bands and Booze on the Festival Express of 1970

podcast.title: Reunion Rehearsal Foundation
podcast.body: John Frusciante suggested that the Red Hot Chili Peppers learn old blues songs as a foundational exercise during their reunion. This was part of a strategy to start from scratch and build basic rock and roll building blocks, making the songwriting process feel more natural. "He was like, let's learn some old blue songs and let's learn some really old red hot chili pepper songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Role in Early Rock and Roll Development
podcast.body: The conventional understanding that rock and roll primarily originated from the guitar-playing male solo artists of the Chicago sound and Delta Bluesmen is challenged. Early rock and roll had relatively little direct influence from this specific branch of the blues, drawing more significantly from Western Swing, Jump Blues, and Vocal Group R&B. "And that's because the common narrative that Muck and Rill came from that kind of blues is false"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Slow-Burn Ballad Inspiration
podcast.body: The song "Shake a Hand" by Fay Adams is identified as the key inspiration for "almost all slow-burn blues ballads in this period," demonstrating its foundational role in a specific subgenre of blues and R&B music. "Shake a Hand if you can."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Source of Floating Lyrics
podcast.body: Carl Perkins' "Matchbox" incorporates "floating lyrics" found in various traditional blues songs, such as the verse "I'm a poor boy and I'm a long way from home" from the song "Poor Boy, Long Way From Home." This demonstrates the influence of traditional blues on early rockabilly and rock and roll. "Instead he uses floating lyrics that one can find in all sorts of other blues songs."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Steam Train Rhythm Influence
podcast.body: The mechanical rhythm of steam trains was a key influence on blues, rhythm and blues, and rock and roll. Rock and roll's emergence coincided with America's shift from a train culture to a car culture, with trains symbolizing freedom and escape in the 1940s and early 50s, a sentiment enshrined in the backbeat of songs like "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie." "That mechanical steam train rhythm is one of the key influences in blues, rhythm and blues, and rock and roll."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 4: "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie" by Louis Jordan

podcast.title: Stop-Time Blues Riff
podcast.body: The "stop-time blues riff" is a distinctive musical phrase that first appeared in Muddy Waters' 1954 song "Hoochie Coochie Man." Songwriters Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller developed an "obsession" with this riff, consistently employing it as a "signifier of the blues" in their compositions for various artists, which significantly contributed to its widespread recognition as a generic indicator of the genre. "Libre and Stuller had latched onto that riff."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Strong Feeling in Jump Bands
podcast.body: A strong blues feeling was a crucial component successfully integrated with boogie, jump, and jive sounds by Lucky Millinder's band, which is considered an early rhythm and blues group, to create music specifically for dancing. "able to combine all the boogie, jump, and give sounds with a strong blues feeling and get people dancing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Sun Records' Archival Releases
podcast.body: The British reissue label Charlie, through the work of Martin Hawkins and Colin Escott, systematically released Sun Records' extensive archives, which included many blues recordings alongside rockabilly. "Especially once a British reissue label called Charlie, employed Martin Hawkins and Colin Escott, two young music obsessives, to put out systematic releases of sons Rocket Billy and Blues Arcames."
